1.pericope_label: Why standest thou afar off? The complaint of God’s distance and the indictment of the proud

schools.summary: Henry turns the complaint back on the complainer: outward deliverance is afar off and hidden from us, and then we think God afar off and want inward comfort, but that is our own fault, for we judge by outward appearance, standing afar off from God by our unbelief and then complaining that he stands afar off from us. He notes that God’s withdrawings are grievous to his people at any time but especially in times of trouble, and that David brings the evil report of the transgressors to his heavenly Father not in any way of vain-glory nor out of personal resentment. Spurgeon answers the same complaint with an image: to the tearful eye of the sufferer the Lord seemed to stand still, as if he calmly looked on and did not sympathise, and appeared no longer a very present help but an inaccessible mountain — yet the refiner is never far from the mouth of the furnace when his gold is in the fire, and the Son of God is always walking in the midst of the flames when his holy children are cast into them; it is not the trouble, he adds, but the hiding of our Father’s face which cuts us to the quick. On the second verse he reads the psalm forensically, finding a formal indictment which divides into the two charges of pride and tyranny, the one the root and cause of the other, followed by the humble petition of the oppressed; and he defends the justice of that petition on the ground that men should be done by as they wished to do to others, since we only weigh them in their own scales and measure their corn with their own bushel.

Augustine makes the delay deliberate and pedagogical. He has the psalmist ask as if all on a sudden he understood, or as if he asked though he knew, that he might teach; and the answer is that God despises seasonably, in tribulations, causing them to inflame men’s minds with longing for his coming, since that fountain of life is sweeter to them that have much thirst. He presses the same principle further than the others would, finding in it the reason why even heresies are permitted to exist — not that heretics wish it, but because divine providence works that result from their sins, ordaining the darkness so that by comparison the light may be the more pleasant, as by comparison with heretics the discovery of truth is the more sweet.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that this and one other are the only anonymous psalms in the first book, and defend the Septuagint’s joining of it to the preceding psalm as not without a certain amount of warrant: both are laid out in tetrastichs, the preceding psalm begins at the beginning of the alphabet while this one begins in the middle with the letter that continues the order, and the letters that should come between are passed over without being introduced acrostically, though their number exactly answers to them. On the second verse they attend to the boasting, that far from hiding the shameful desire of his soul the wicked man makes it an object and ground of high and sounding praise, imagining himself above all restraint human or divine; and they reject Hupfeld’s rendering of the following clause outright, holding that the persecutor is himself the covetous or rapacious person the verse names. Ellicott would render the opening of the second verse differently from the received text, that in the pride of the wicked the sufferer burns, following the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus and the Vulgate, and insists the word is not of indignation felt by the sufferers but literally of the afflictions they endure; in the next clause he takes the humble rather than the wicked as the subject, since that preserves the parallelism better and agrees with the rest of the psalm, so that the sufferers are taken in the plot which the wicked have devised.

Calvin keeps the psalm David’s own, complaining in his own name and in the name of all the godly that fraud, extortion, cruelty, violence and all kind of injustice prevailed everywhere, and assigning as the cause that ungodly men, intoxicated with their prosperity, have shaken off all fear of God and think they may do what they please with impunity. He reads the whole as a mirror in which is seen a lively image of a widely corrupt and disorganised state of society, into which the children of God should learn to look when iniquity breaks out like a flood, lest the strangeness of such a temptation shake their faith and cast them into despair; it tends greatly to lighten grief, he says, to consider that nothing befalls us at this day which the Church of God has not experienced in the days of old. Gill begins from the doctrine of omnipresence, that God by his infinite essence and power is everywhere and never far from any of his creatures, so that when he stands afar off it is in their apprehension only, when he withdraws his gracious presence and defers help; and he reads the verb of the second verse with the Jewish commentators as following after and pursuing hotly, which denotes the vehemence and heat of the persecutor’s fury. He alone looks past the immediate oppressor to a figure, making the wicked one the lawless one, the man of sin and son of perdition, the great persecutor of Christ’s poor saints and faithful witnesses.

Clarke reaches the joining of the two psalms from the manuscripts rather than the acrostic, noting that this psalm forms part of the preceding in the Vulgate and Septuagint and in several of the collated codices; but he departs from the rest on the occasion, taking it to belong to the time of the captivity or the return of the captives, and probably composed with reference to Sanballat and the other enemies of the Jews. On the enmity itself he declines to explain it on any principle of nature or reason, concluding that the devil hates godliness and the wicked man hates it because the devil is in his heart.

debates.question: Why does God seem to stand afar off?

positions.view: He is everywhere by his essence; the distance is in their apprehension, when he withdraws gracious presence and defers help
It is our own fault: we judge by outward appearance and stand afar off from God by unbelief
He is near though unseen, as the refiner never leaves the furnace mouth while his gold is in the fire
He despises seasonably, causing tribulation to inflame longing for his coming

debates.question: What is the occasion and authorship of the psalm?

positions.view: David’s own, in his name and all the godly’s, a mirror of a corrupt society
Of the captivity or the return, probably with reference to Sanballat and the enemies of the Jews
Anonymous; joined to the preceding psalm by the Septuagint, and the acrostic supports it

debates.question: Who burns, and who is taken in the devices?

positions.view: In the pride of the wicked the sufferer burns, of afflictions endured, not indignation felt; and the sufferers are taken in the plot the wicked devised
The wicked pursues hotly, the verb denoting the heat of his fury

outliers.claim: Alone in extending the principle of seasonable delay to the permission of heresies, which providence ordains as darkness so that the light may be the more pleasant.
Alone in reading the wicked one as the man of sin and son of perdition rather than a contemporary oppressor.
Alone in reading the second verse as a formal legal indictment followed by a petition, and in defending the petition’s justice by the measure men used to others.

themes: Why standest thou afar off, O LORD? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?
The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor
let them be taken in the devices that they have imagined

3.pericope_label: The portrait of the wicked: his boasting, his security, his ambushes and his lion’s patience

schools.summary: Gill surveys four renderings of the phrase about the wicked man’s ways, that they cause terror and make men fear, or are defiled as the Greek and Latin have it, or always remain the same with no change in them for the better, or else prosper, which he notes is sometimes stumbling to the saints. On the lurking places he observes that the word signifies palaces or courts, as the Chaldee and Syriac render it, so that the allusion is not to mean thieves and robbers at all but to persons of note and figure, the Greek and Latin and Arabic and Ethiopic versions giving that he sits in lurking places with the rich. Of the refusal to seek God he notes that the supplement is supported by the Targum and Kimchi, and that it is the character of every unregenerate man not to seek God for counsel nor to inquire into his will but to do what seems best in his own eyes. Throughout the portrait he alone reads an allegory, finding the mouth of the first beast and the speech of the second, the insidious methods of a power which has two horns like a lamb and yet calls itself the servant of servants, and whose ways he traces through boasting of universal power, of infallibility, and of signs and lying wonders.

Ellicott spends much of this portrait correcting the received translation. On the boast he gives the literal sense as speaking praise to the lust of his own soul, allowing that it has been understood either as priding himself upon his evil desires or, with the Septuagint and Vulgate and Syriac and Chaldee, as priding himself according to his sinful wish; he finds the representation of a villain addressing his evil passions in laudatory terms highly poetic, comparing the rich fool of the parable who congratulates his soul upon his greed, and where the English has blessing the covetous he reads cursing instead, by a common euphemism. On the next verse he says roundly that the Authorised Version has quite missed the meaning, and would render that the wicked in his haughtiness — literally the height of his nostril — says God will not requite it, and that there is no God in all his thought. For the ways he prefers that his enterprises always succeed, taking the sense from a cognate meaning strength and from a parallel in Job, though he allows that always strong may imply only the bold and reckless course with which a tyrant pursues his end. The lurking places he takes properly of enclosed spaces and then of any collection of dwellings, noting the word is used elsewhere of an unwalled place and even of a nomadic encampment, and he calls the lion and the net a confusion of metaphor, the wicked being first the lion watching for prey and then the hunter snaring animals. Keil and Delitzsch secure the sense of lasting or stiff for the same disputed verb from that passage in Job: he takes whatever ways he chooses and they always lead to the desired end, so that he neither stumbles nor goes astray. They describe the strophe as one of only three lines which sets out a happiness he allows nothing to disturb, read the wicked man’s boundless carnal security as giving free course to his tongue, so that he says in godless self-confidence what the believer may say by reason of fellowship with God, and see the figure of the lion reversed in the second line of the later verse.

Clarke reads the boast as made among his fellows, how often he has gratified such and such passions in such and such circumstances, which shows the excess of a depraved and imbruted spirit; he who can boast of his iniquity is in the broad road to perdition, and should such a one repent it would be equal to any miracle. He redivides the following clause to different effect from Ellicott, so that it is the wicked man who abhors the Lord rather than the Lord who abhors the covetous: those like himself he commends and associates with, and they have a mortal hatred of everything holy. Of the ways he offers something quite different again, that the man is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times, conceiving and bringing forth sin until death is brought forth with it; and he finds in the ambush verses an allusion to espionage, the setting of spies on a man’s conduct, or the conduct of an assassin and private murderer, likening him also to a hunter who lays traps and gins, digs pits and sets nets. He reads the refusal to seek God as pride, the man too proud to bend his knee before his Judge and too haughty to put on sackcloth. Wesley keeps the highwayman, placing him not within the villages but in the ways bordering upon them or leading to them, as robbers use to do, and glossing the hidden eyes as watching and looking out from the lurking place. He notes that pride is properly seated in the heart but manifest in the countenance, that the man glories in his very sins which are his shame, and that the judgments he disregards are the threatenings denounced against sinners, which he despises as though he could blow them away with a breath, a gesture of contempt in scripture and other authors alike.

debates.question: What does it mean that his ways are always grievous?

positions.view: Four possibilities: they cause terror, or are defiled, or always remain the same, or prosper
Better, his enterprises always succeed; or perhaps only that his ways are always strong
He is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times
Lasting or stiff: his chosen ways always reach the desired end and he never stumbles

debates.question: What sort of man lurks in the lurking places?

positions.view: A person of note and figure, the word meaning palaces or courts; the versions give that he sits with the rich
Enclosed spaces, any collection of dwellings, even an unwalled place or a nomadic encampment
A highwayman, in the ways bordering on the villages, as robbers use to do
A spy or private assassin; and a hunter with traps, gins, pits and nets

debates.question: Does the clause say the LORD abhors the covetous, or that the wicked abhors the LORD?

positions.view: Read "curseth" by a common euphemism rather than "blesseth"
He blesseth the covetous, and he abhorreth the LORD

outliers.claim: Alone in rendering the disputed phrase of travail, the wicked man in pain to bring forth iniquity until death comes with it.
Alone in saying outright that the Authorised Version has quite missed the meaning of a verse here, and alone in naming the lion and the net a confusion of metaphor.
Alone in carrying an allegorical reading of a single oppressor through the whole portrait.

themes: For the wicked boasteth of his heart’s desire, and blesseth the covetous, whom the LORD abhorreth
The wicked, through the pride of his countenance, will not seek after God: God is not in all his thoughts
His ways are always grievous: thy judgments are far above out of his sight
He hath said in his heart, I shall not be moved: for I shall never be in adversity
His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity
He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent
He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor
He hath said in his heart, God hath forgotten: he hideth his face; he will never see it

12.pericope_label: Arise, O LORD: the plea that God has seen, and the petition to break the oppressor’s arm

schools.summary: Spurgeon marks the boldness of the prayer and its inconsistency together: with what bold language will faith address its God, and yet what unbelief is mingled with our strongest confidence, since the Lord is fearlessly stirred up to arise and lift up his hand and then timidly begged not to forget the humble, as if Jehovah could ever be forgetful of his saints; the verse, he adds, is the incessant cry of the Church, from which she will never refrain until her Lord comes in his glory to avenge her of all her adversaries. On the following verses he holds that the description of the wicked is condensed and the evil of his character traced to its source, namely atheistical ideas with regard to the government of the world, so that the whole is another urgent plea for God to show his power and reveal his justice: when the wicked call God’s righteousness in question, we may well beg him to teach them terrible things in righteousness. Henry asks for something more final than a warning, that God would arise to the confusion of those who say he hides his face, manifest his presence and providence in the affairs of this lower world, and lift up his hand to give a fatal blow to the oppressors, his everlasting arm being made bare; and he grounds the whole address upon the foregoing representation of the inhumanity and impiety of those oppressors.

Clarke reads the lifting up of the hand as a threat rather than a stroke, that God would hear their reproaches and see their guile and consider his oppressed people, and threaten the wicked so that they may desist and repent, and only if they repent not let them be punished. He turns the delay itself into mercy, asking how the Lord permits such persons to triumph in their iniquity and answering that the longsuffering of God leads them to repentance. On the assurance that God has seen he says nothing can escape his notice and that he has not forgotten his justice though judgment is not speedily executed on an evil work, and of the poor man he says that to God he has given up his body, his soul and his cause, in the full conviction that the helper of the fatherless will not forget him. On the last petition he offers two renderings without choosing between them, that the man’s haunts shall all be investigated and punishment continue while there is a crime to punish, or else that God will continue to judge and punish transgressors till not one is to be found. Wesley puts the question of permission far more sharply than Clarke, as a charge rather than an inquiry: why dost thou, by giving them impunity, suffer and occasion them to despise thee? Of the last petition he takes it of searching out wickedness and punishing these wicked atheists until no such wickedness be left in the world, or at least in the church.

Ellicott notes in passing that the acrostic arrangement is resumed at this verse with the letter koph, which bears on the question of the psalm’s relation to the one before it. On the committing of the helpless to God he alone will not leave the text as it stands: he would render that the helpless leaveth it to Thee, and then observes that by a slight alteration in the division of the Hebrew letters and of the pointing we should get something quite different, that it is against Thee that he is strong in darkness, which turns the clause from the sufferer’s trust into the oppressor’s defiance. On the last petition he holds the sense clear from two passages elsewhere, where to seek and not find is a proverb expressing the riddance of evil, though he grants the construction is difficult, would end the first clause at the word wicked and take the following words absolutely, and renders that as for the evil man, thou shalt look for his wickedness and not find it. Keil and Delitzsch answer the wicked man’s premise directly, that it is with God entirely different from what the ungodly imagine: they think he will not punish, but he does see, and the psalmist knows and confesses it, the perfect tense meaning that God has seen and does see what is done to his own. On the last petition they oppose Ellicott’s proverb outright, holding it a mistake to regard the two verbs of the verse as correlative notions, because in the phrase to seek and not find, used of that which has totally disappeared, the Hebrew never employs the verb standing here but always a different one — and they cite for this the very same two passages on which the proverbial reading is built.

Gill defines what it is to contemn God: his being, perfections and providence are denied or called in question or abused, his word is derided, the great things of his law counted a strange thing and the truths of his Gospel reckoned foolishness, while the decrees and doctrines and traditions of men are set up in their place. On the assurance that God has seen he presses the omniscience, that though the wicked say God will never see, he sees all things in general, all men and all their actions, and everything in particular, even that which is said or thought in the heart. Of the breaking of the arm he takes it of the oppressor’s power and strength, so that he shall not be able to hold the sword or strike a blow or do any hurt to the people of God, and judges the prayer already in some measure fulfilled, the power being weakened and the arm broken though the kingdom is not yet broken to pieces.

debates.question: What is asked when God is bidden lift up his hand?

positions.view: A fatal blow to the oppressors, and his everlasting arm made bare
A threat, that they may desist and repent; punishment only if they repent not

debates.question: Why does God suffer the wicked to contemn him?

positions.view: His longsuffering leads them to repentance
Put as a charge: by giving them impunity God suffers and occasions them to despise him
The contempt springs from atheistical ideas about the government of the world
They think he will not punish, but he does see, and the psalmist knows it

debates.question: Is "seek out his wickedness till thou find none" a proverb of riddance?

positions.view: Yes: the sense is clear from two parallel passages where to seek and not find expresses riddance of evil
No: the two verbs are not correlative, and those very parallels use a different verb from the one standing here

outliers.claim: Alone in noticing that the prayer is internally inconsistent, bold in stirring God up and then timid in begging him not to forget.
Alone in proposing a redivision of the Hebrew letters that would turn the sufferer’s committing of himself to God into the oppressor’s being strong against God in darkness.

themes: Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up thine hand: forget not the humble
Wherefore doth the wicked contemn God? he hath said in his heart, Thou wilt not require it
Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand
the poor committeth himself unto thee: thou art the helper of the fatherless
Break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil man: seek out his wickedness till thou find none

16.pericope_label: The LORD is King for ever: the heathen perished, the humble heard, the oppressed judged

schools.summary: Ellicott puts the change of key briefly, that if the psalm has hitherto been personal it here swells out into a larger strain of national hope and faith. On the final line he takes the words quite otherwise than Clarke, rendering literally that he may not continue to terrify, or to defy, mere man from the earth, which he thinks may mean that mere mortals shall have to confess their weakness; and on the oppressed of the same verse he borrows a sentence from Leighton, that God’s choice acquaintances are humble men. Keil and Delitzsch describe the poet as standing on an eminence from which he seems to behold the end, basking in the realisation of what has been obtained in answer to prayer, the ardent longing of the meek and lowly sufferers for the arising of the Lord having now been heard, and under circumstances which the psalm goes on to express.

Spurgeon reads the close as a song of thanksgiving to the great and everlasting King, because he has granted the desire of his humble and oppressed people, defended the fatherless and punished the heathen who trampled upon his poor and afflicted children; from which he draws that we are sure to speed well if we carry our complaint to the King of kings, since rights will be vindicated and wrongs redressed at his throne, and his government neither neglects the interests of the needy nor tolerates oppression in the mighty.

Wesley grounds the comfort in the office itself, that it belongs to a king to protect his subjects, so that his people’s case is never desperate while he ever lives to help them; the heathen he takes for the Canaanites whom God as king of the world expelled to give their land to his people, and the land he calls God’s because he gave it to them and fixed his presence and dwelling in it, the whole standing as a great example by which faith and hope are confirmed for the future. Clarke agrees the heathen may refer to the Canaanites, adding that they were either cut off or converted, and then turns the verse upon his own country, that once it was entirely heathen and now there is not one heathen family in the whole land. On the preparing of the heart he sets out an economy of grace in four steps, that God prepares the heart, suggests the prayer, hears what is prayed and answers the petition, concluding that a man with a cry in his heart after God may rest assured it proceeded from a divine preparation, that no man ever had such a cry after salvation but from God, and that he who continues to cry shall infallibly be heard. On the last line he believes the Hebrew better rendered that the oppressor may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land, so that the prayer is for the tyrant’s influence to be destroyed and for him never again to have power to add even one further act of oppression; and he applies it to those who, for their religion’s sake and because they would serve God with a pure conscience, have been driven off their farms and turned out of their houses by wicked lords and arrogant landowners.

Gill looks forward rather than back, taking the King to be Christ, who was King from everlasting and was promised and prophesied of as King under the old dispensation, who had a kingdom on earth though not of this world, who at his ascension and session at the right hand of God appeared more visibly in his kingly office, and of whom it will be yet more manifest in the latter day that he is King of saints. On the hearing of desire he observes that the prayers of God’s people sometimes lie in inward and secret desires of the soul and are not expressed in words, that these desires are all before the Lord and well known to him, that such prayers of the heart are principally regarded by him, and that they are his own preparation. Of the final verse he reads the judging of the fatherless and oppressed as God avenging the wrongs done to them by the man of sin.

debates.question: Who are the heathen perished out of his land?

positions.view: The Canaanites, expelled by God as king of the world to give their land to his people
The Canaanites perhaps, cut off or converted — and the verse applies to his own once-heathen country
Read forward instead: the King is Christ, whose kingly office will be yet more manifest in the latter day

debates.question: What does the last line ask?

positions.view: That the oppressor may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land
Literally, that he may not continue to terrify or defy mere man from the earth
That God avenge the wrongs done to the fatherless and those oppressed by the man of sin

outliers.claim: Alone in applying the perishing of the heathen to his own country, and alone in applying the closing petition to tenants evicted from their farms for conscience’ sake.
Alone in quoting Leighton, and alone in reading the last line of defying mere man from the earth rather than driving the poor off the land.

themes: The LORD is King for ever and ever: the heathen are perished out of his land
LORD, thou hast heard the desire of the humble: thou wilt prepare their heart, thou wilt cause thine ear to hear
To judge the fatherless and the oppressed, that the man of the earth may no more oppress
